Maladaptive Strategies.value: make sure to stay close to exit
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

vignette:
Daniel Weber was 34 when he came for treatment, a married firefighter who had spent part of the previous year deployed as a relief worker in a war zone. He described the shift that stayed with him in plain, clipped detail. His team had been moving civilians through a damaged public building that was being used as a temporary aid site. The mood had been tense but organized until shouting broke out near the entrance and the crowd surged in a way that made the room feel suddenly unstable. Daniel remembered how quickly ordinary features of the space became matters of survival: where the doors were, how many people stood between him and them, which corners offered cover, who was moving toward him and who might be carrying a threat. Men he did not know came toward the building in the confusion, and in those seconds he could not tell who needed help and who meant harm. He had to keep working while bracing for the possibility that the next person through the doorway might be dangerous. He recalled feeling that there was nowhere in the room to settle his attention except on routes out and the movements of strangers.

When he returned to the United States and resumed work at his firehouse, those moments did not feel finished. He noticed it first in enclosed places. The instant he entered a grocery store, a restaurant, a station briefing room, even his own living room after stepping in from outside, his eyes moved automatically to the exits. He could not seem to stop himself from calculating how quickly he could get out if something happened. If he and his wife met friends for dinner, Daniel chose the chair with the clearest line to the door or stayed standing near the edge of the room until he could orient himself. He knew this looked odd, and sometimes rude, but being away from an exit left him too keyed up to follow a conversation. At work, even in familiar municipal buildings during routine calls, he found himself checking entryways and secondary exits before he could focus on the task in front of him.

He also felt newly wary of strangers in ordinary situations. A customer stepping too close in line at a convenience store, a man approaching him in a parking lot to ask a question, someone entering the fire station unexpectedly-these encounters produced a jolt of threat that Daniel experienced in his body before he had time to think. What unsettled him most was how little the setting mattered. He could be home on his own street, taking out the trash or walking from the driveway to the front door, and still feel on guard, as if safety were conditional and could vanish without warning. Inside the house, he checked where the doors were from room to room and paid attention to sounds outside in a way that left him unable to fully settle. He did not describe his home as dangerous, exactly; it was more that he no longer trusted the feeling of being protected there.

Over the following months, he began shaping his life around this constant readiness. Before deployment, he had relied on exercise to manage stress, but afterward he stopped. The physical sensations of exertion-pounding heart, shortness of breath, heat in his body-felt too close to the state of alarm he was already fighting to contain. He told himself he was just busy, but he knew he was avoiding it because it made him feel exposed and revved up. He also began pulling back from moments that should have felt good. When his wife suggested a weekend away, or when a rare calm evening at home started to feel pleasant, Daniel caught himself shutting it down internally. He had come to believe that letting himself feel happy or relaxed was unsafe, as if lowering his guard even briefly would leave him unprepared. He would become quieter, change the subject, or busy himself with chores, leaving his wife confused by how quickly warmth seemed to disappear from him.

These habits narrowed his world in ways that became harder to ignore. His wife noticed that he always steered them toward seats near exits and that he seemed more tense, not less, when they were in the safety of their own home. At the firehouse, where readiness was part of the job, his constant scanning could pass unnoticed for a time, but Daniel knew it had become different from ordinary vigilance. Even in routine downtime with his crew, he could not simply sit with his back to a room and relax. He was tired of living as though every doorway might become a danger point and every unfamiliar face a possible threat.

What finally brought him in was not one dramatic incident but the accumulation of these daily constrictions. His wife told him she missed being able to reach him when they were together, and Daniel recognized the truth of that. He said he wanted help because he was exhausted by feeling on guard in places that were supposed to be safe. At the same time, he was afraid that if he stopped scanning exits, stopped staying near doors, stopped pushing away relief or happiness, he would be caught off guard and fail to protect himself or the people around him. What he hoped for, carefully stated, was not to become careless, but to be at home, at work, and with his wife without feeling as if danger were already in the room.
